#9982. Amazon S3 Tables now offer managed migration of Apache Hive tables to Apache Iceberg

AWS is the world's most comprehensive cloud, enabling organizations to accelerate innovation, reduce costs, and scale more efficiently

Migrate to modernize → Modernize to unlock data → unlock data to run AI

Get started with one of these featured services or browse all

From startups to enterprises, find AWS solutions scaled to your needs. Access tailored resources, pricing models, and support levels.

Today, we’re announcing a simple, cost-effective path for data lake modernization. Amazon S3 Tables now support managed migration of your Apache Hive tables to Apache Iceberg. Migration works with Parquet tables in Amazon S3 that are registered in the AWS Glue Data Catalog and allows you to upgrade your data lake with no pipelines to build or compute to provision, while production workloads keep running.

Apache Iceberg has become the open standard for large analytics datasets. It lets you manage petabyte-scale tables with features like schema evolution, hidden partitioning, and time travel queries, while keeping your data open and queryable with any Iceberg-compatible engine. Amazon S3 Tables offer fully managed storage purpose-built to keep Iceberg tables performant and cost-effective as they grow, with features like automatic maintenance, optimization, replication, and S3 Intelligent-Tiering built-in.

What is new Previously, migrating Apache Hive tables to Apache Iceberg could take weeks of engineering work to build and manage the required infrastructure. Converting data types and building rollback capabilities added operational complexity. Now, this is available as a managed, API-driven operation.

S3 Tables handle the entire migration workflow, including data validation, compatibility checks, type conversions, file recompression, and compaction. Before copying any data, S3 Tables identify every source object in scope and generate a compatibility report. You can sync as many times as you need without stopping writes to your source table, except for a few minutes during cutover. Once you are ready, you can complete the migration, minimizing time that tables are offline.

Compared to self-managed approaches, S3 Tables managed migrations are cost-effective because you pay only for the data copied, with no charge for the Hive-to-Iceberg conversion, and source objects in S3 Intelligent-Tiering stay in their current access tier.

A first look at the migration To migrate an AWS Glue Hive table, choose your destination table bucket in the S3 console, then choose Create table from migration.

Create a namespace and table name for your destination Iceberg table. The destination table is created using recommended default settings tuned for query performance and storage efficiency.

When you start the migration, S3 Tables validate the source table, generate a compatibility report, and begin copying data. The destination table is read-only during the migration. Once you complete migration, the destination table is promoted to read-write.

You can begin working with your data right away using a direct integration with Amazon Athena and Amazon SageMaker Unified Studio in the AWS console, or use any tool compatible with the Apache Iceberg REST API to directly query the tables. To learn more, visit the S3 Tables migration documentation.

You can also use AWS Command Line Interface (AWS CLI), AWS SDKs, or the Agent Toolkit for AWS. For example, set up migration jobs and call the start-table-migration command.

To catch up the destination table with changes in the source, call sync-table-migration as many times as you need before you complete the migration. Each sync copies only what changed.

If you’re using coding agents like Kiro, the migrating-hive-tables-to-s3-tables skill in the Agent Toolkit for AWS provides step-by-step migration guidance with safety guardrails for agents. The skill can:

To learn more, visit the GitHub README page for the skill.

Now available Amazon S3 Tables managed migration is available today in US East (N. Virginia, Ohio), US West (Oregon), Asia Pacific (Mumbai, Singapore, Sydney, Tokyo), and Europe (Frankfurt, Ireland, Stockholm) Regions. At launch, the capability supports AWS Glue-registered Hive tables stored in Parquet format within the same AWS account and AWS Region. If you want to call APIs, search documentation, find regional availability, or troubleshoot about this new feature, try using the AWS MCP Server and plugins with your preferred AI tool.

Try it in the Amazon S3 console today and send feedback to AWS re:Post for Amazon S3 or through your usual AWS Support contacts.

#9978. AWS Weekly Roundup: AgentCore Runtime V2, Amazon DynamoDB bulk put items, and more (November 9, 2026)

AWS is the world's most comprehensive cloud, enabling organizations to accelerate innovation, reduce costs, and scale more efficiently

Migrate to modernize → Modernize to unlock data → unlock data to run AI

Get started with one of these featured services or browse all

From startups to enterprises, find AWS solutions scaled to your needs. Access tailored resources, pricing models, and support levels.

Most of the cost of adopting something new isn’t the new thing, it’s the move. Moving a Hive table to Apache Iceberg has typically meant weeks of engineering work. Last week, Amazon S3 Tables turned that into three steps: start, sync as often as you need, complete. The source stays writable except for a few minutes at cutover. The same week, Amazon DynamoDB started loading data from S3 into tables that already exist.

The pattern I like is that neither one asks you to stop what’s running. That’s also the way to read the agent news this week. The new Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Runtime is a single field on the runtime you already have, and Web Answer is a tool you attach to a gateway you already run. Now, let’s get into this week’s AWS news…

HeadlinesThe new AgentCore Runtime: elastic, optimized, and consistently fast starts – If you run agents on AgentCore and haven’t tried the new runtime since it became generally available, it’s worth a look. It changes two things. First, memory: sessions start small, page in more on demand, and give memory back when it goes cold instead of holding the peak, so you pay for what your agent uses. Second, cold starts: AgentCore prepares your environment once, snapshots it, and restores the snapshot for every new instance. In the team’s tests, that kept P75 cold starts at about 2 seconds for images from 200 MB up to 2 GB, while the original runtime rose from roughly 5.4 seconds to nearly 30 seconds as images grew. The per-unit rate is higher, but you use far fewer GB-hours, so the team expects most agents to see a lower bill, though that isn’t guaranteed.

To opt in, you set platformVersion to V2 when you create or update a runtime. Create and update take several minutes while the snapshot is prepared, and your container must report healthy on /ping within 120 seconds, so report health only after initialization finishes. The docs cover how to optimize your agent for V2. V2 is available in 10 Regions, and committed baseline pricing is coming soon.

Amazon S3 Tables now offer managed migration of Apache Hive tables to Apache Iceberg – You can now migrate Parquet tables registered in the AWS Glue Data Catalog into S3 Tables without building a pipeline or provisioning compute. S3 Tables validates the source and produces a compatibility report covering every object in scope. Each sync copies only what changed, so production keeps writing until cutover. Afterward you can query the table with Amazon Athena, Amazon SageMaker Unified Studio, or any engine that speaks the Iceberg REST API. You pay only for the data copied, with no charge for the conversion, and objects in S3 Intelligent-Tiering keep their tier. At launch it works within the same account and Region, in 10 Regions.

Last week’s launches Here are some launches and updates from this past week that caught my attention:

Amazon DynamoDB now supports bulk put items – You can now load line-delimited DynamoDB JSON or Amazon Ion files from Amazon S3 into existing tables as a managed, asynchronous job. Each record can carry its own condition expression, so one file can mix plain, insert-only, and version-guarded writes. Writes use dedicated system capacity and cost less than the equivalent per-request writes. An Accelerated tier handles deadline-bound jobs. The Database blog post gives illustrative Accelerated times of less than 1 hour for 100 million 1 KB items. One thing to know before you start: canceling doesn’t roll back items already written.

Announcing Web Answer on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore – You can now give an agent a single tool call that returns a synthesized, cited answer to a natural-language question, instead of building your own search, retrieval, and citation pipeline. Web Answer plans its own searches, runs several in parallel, and decides when it has enough evidence. You attach it as a target on AgentCore Gateway and call it over MCP, and you can limit it with domain include and deny lists and publish-date filters. It’s available in US East (N. Virginia). The getting started post explains when to use it instead of Web Search, which returns ranked results for your own model to synthesize.

AWS Lambda now supports queues for Apache Kafka in self-managed Kafka event sources – You can now process records from a single Kafka partition across many parallel AWS Lambda invocations. Classic consumer groups cap parallelism at the partition count. Queue mode uses Kafka share groups and needs Kafka 4.2 or later with share groups enabled. It works with self-managed clusters and managed offerings such as Confluent Cloud. You give up ordering and get at-least-once delivery, so your functions need to be idempotent. The Compute blog walkthrough covers poller scaling and when to keep stream mode.

AWS announces AWS Interconnect – last mile preview with Equinix – You can now set up a private, managed connection from Equinix’s network of 282 data centers to AWS without ordering cross-connects or configuring routers. Capacity is quad-redundant across two locations and four links, with BGP and VLANs configured for you, a 99.99% availability SLA, and MACsec by default. You pick a Region, bandwidth, and AWS Direct Connect gateway, then paste the activation key into Equinix Fabric. The preview covers the San Jose metro and, as of last Thursday, Northern Virginia, with 1 Gbps connections at no charge.

AWS Security Hub now provides an SBOM inventory for your compute resources – You can now see every software package installed across your organization’s Amazon EC2 instances, Amazon ECR images, and Lambda functions in AWS Security Hub, with each package’s version and how many resources run it. That’s the list you want the next time a widely used library has a vulnerability. The inventory builds on the SBOMs that Amazon Inspector already generates, so it fills in automatically wherever Inspector is enabled. It’s included in Security Hub Essentials at no additional cost.

For a full list of AWS announcements, be sure to keep an eye on the What’s New with AWS page.

Other AWS news Here are some additional posts and resources that you might find interesting:

Serverless ICYMI Q3 2026 – Julian Wood’s quarterly recap is a quick serverless catch-up before re:Invent: Lambda SnapStart for container images, a 90-minute timeout on Lambda Managed Instances, Lambda MicroVMs in 10 Regions, 1 MiB payloads in Amazon SNS, and the new AgentCore Runtime.

AWS contributes a large-transaction binary log optimization to MySQL – With binlog on, a huge transaction holds a global commit lock while its events are copied, blocking every other commit. The optimization, which Amazon Aurora MySQL has run in production since 2019, promotes the spill file into the binlog instead of copying it. In AWS’s tests, commit latency for a 50 GiB transaction dropped from about 7 minutes to about 2 to 2.5 seconds. It has now shipped to community MySQL.

How OrderServ achieved up to 64% cost savings with multi-tenant ECS – Cognizant’s food-ordering platform went from one Amazon ECS cluster per brand on AWS Fargate to a shared cluster on EC2 Auto Scaling groups with warm pools. The 64% applies to a 3-year Compute Savings Plan (47% with a 1-year plan). Scaling time also fell from 5–7 minutes to 30–60 seconds.

Upcoming AWS events Check your calendar and sign up for upcoming AWS events:

AWS re:Invent – re:Invent returns to Las Vegas from November 30 to December 4. The event catalog is live and reserved seating is open, so register and claim your spots before they fill up.

AWS Community Days – Community-led conferences planned and delivered by community leaders, with a few more before the year ends: Belém, Brazil (November 14), JAWS FESTA 2026 in Akita, Japan (November 17), and Port Harcourt, Nigeria (December 12).

Join the AWS Builder Center to connect with builders, share solutions, and access content that supports your development. Browse here for upcoming AWS-led in-person and virtual events and developer-focused events.

That’s all for this week. Check back next Monday for another Weekly Roundup!

This post is part of our Weekly Roundup series. Check back each week for a quick roundup of interesting news and announcements from AWS!

Daniel Abib is a senior specialist solutions architect at AWS, focused on generative AI and Amazon Bedrock — and passionate about serverless. He helps startups and enterprises build AI-powered applications and modernize with cloud-native architectures. A three-time Ironman finisher and four-time re:Invent speaker, he brings the same endurance mindset to building cloud solutions.

#9976. Test your applications against AWS locally with AWS Emulator

AWS is the world's most comprehensive cloud, enabling organizations to accelerate innovation, reduce costs, and scale more efficiently

Migrate to modernize → Modernize to unlock data → unlock data to run AI

Get started with one of these featured services or browse all

From startups to enterprises, find AWS solutions scaled to your needs. Access tailored resources, pricing models, and support levels.

Today we’re announcing AWS Emulator, a local emulator for Amazon Web Services (AWS) that you run on your machine. The AWS Command Line Interface (AWS CLI), the AWS SDKs, and your coding agents speak to it over a local HTTPS endpoint using the same AWS APIs they would use in the cloud, from your laptop. AWS Emulator has no additional service fee. You pay only for AWS resources when you deploy on AWS. Its source is on GitHub. You install it from an RPM or Debian package on Linux, and on macOS and Windows you run it in Docker.

How it works You install the emulator, start it, and point your tools at the local endpoint. When AWS Emulator starts, it generates its own credentials, a config file, and a certificate, and writes them to ~/.aws/emulator/9297/. You set environment variables so the AWS SDK talks to your laptop instead of AWS, and your application code stays unchanged.

From there, your existing tests, CLI scripts, and coding agents keep working the way they already do. A unit test that creates an Amazon DynamoDB table, writes an item, and reads it back is the same test, and it runs on your machine without a deployment. A coding agent can create resources, check the result, and iterate again without waiting on a deployment in a Region.

The emulator is implemented in Rust so that it stays light on CPU and memory on a laptop. It supports the APIs of AWS services that have an API model in the AWS API models repository on GitHub, and because it’s built from those models, the same ones the AWS SDKs use, your requests and the errors you get back have the same shape as on AWS.

If you are a developer, especially one working with coding agents such as Kiro or Claude Code, you can use that loop to test AWS interactions of real complexity locally.

Let’s try it out To get started, I installed the package on Amazon Linux 2023. The package adds the aws-emulator command to /usr/bin/, so it’s on the path.

On macOS and Windows, you build a Docker image from the short Dockerfile in the documentation and run the emulator in a container. We don’t publish a ready-made image.

I started the emulator with aws-emulator. It serves HTTPS on 127.0.0.1:9297, so only my own computer can reach it, and it writes its log as JSON lines that show the address, the config file, and the certificate file.

In another terminal, I set the environment variables that point the AWS CLI at the emulator, and unset any variables that could supply real AWS credentials.

The emulator generates new keys each time it starts. Its access key IDs start with EMULATOR, so you can’t mistake them for real AWS keys, and it rejects requests signed with any other keys. To confirm that my shell was talking to the emulator, I checked the health endpoint and the caller identity. The emulator uses a single account, 000000000000.

Then I created a bucket, copied in a small object, and listed it.

With the AWS CLI pointed at my laptop, I had the same commands I already use and a local endpoint that answered them.

Next I wanted to see it the way I actually work now, so with the emulator still running I opened Kiro and asked it to create an Amazon DynamoDB table, write an item, and read it back, all against AWS Emulator rather than my AWS account.

To use the same setup with an existing test suite, I would start the emulator, set the same environment variables in the script that runs the tests, and run them as usual.

Using the emulator in process Running the emulator as a local process gives you an HTTPS endpoint that works with the AWS CLI and the AWS SDKs through environment variables. Some SDKs need an extra setting to trust the emulator certificate, for example a trust store for the AWS SDK for Java. For tests, there is a second option. AWS Emulator ships an embedded mode that you instantiate directly inside your test process and wire into the SDK through its HTTP client, rather than talking to a separate server over the network. Each embedded instance keeps its own state, so tests do not share buckets, tables, or queues, and you can run many of them in parallel. Embedded mode is available for the AWS SDK for Rust. You add the aws-emulator-embedded crate from GitHub to the [dev-dependencies] section of your Cargo.toml file. The following example creates an Amazon DynamoDB table, writes an item, and reads it back, entirely in process.

When it runs as a local process, the emulator requires every request to be signed with Signature Version 4 (SigV4), the same way AWS does, and it exposes a /__admin/health endpoint on the same port so a script or a container can wait until it is ready before running tests. By default it also sends anonymous usage and error data, and you can turn it off.

How we measure fidelity An emulator is only useful if a test that passes against it would also pass against AWS, so we measure that directly with fidelity tests. A fidelity test is a short program that uses an AWS SDK to run a workflow, such as storing an object and then reading and deleting it, and asserts how AWS behaves. We verify each fidelity test against real AWS. A fidelity test passes only if the emulator matches AWS on the response to every call, including the status code, the body, and the exact error code and message, and on the resources and data that the workflow creates.

With each release, we publish how many fidelity tests pass for each service, as k of n. For example, 40 of 50 means that 40 of the service’s 50 fidelity tests pass. The set of fidelity tests is public in the aws-emulator-evaluation-suite repository on GitHub, including the ones that don’t pass yet, so you can see what we verified and run the fidelity tests yourself. Read a score as a snapshot of a product that’s improving. When we add fidelity tests, a score can go down even while the emulator gets better.

If the emulator doesn’t implement an operation yet, it returns HTTP 501 (Not Implemented), so your tests fail right away. If the emulator acts differently from AWS, you can tell us by opening an issue in the AWS Emulator repository on GitHub.

How the emulator is built AWS Emulator is built and maintained by agents from the AWS API models using Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Runtime Instances, AWS CodePipeline, and AWS CodeCommit, so it stays current with AWS as those models change.

One group of agents looks for gaps, both by comparing emulator responses against real AWS and by statically comparing the emulator’s code against the published Smithy models, and files an issue for each gap it finds. Another group picks up an issue, writes tests, implements the behavior, and reviews the change for correctness, performance, and security. When the change is ready, it is pushed to a source repository, and that push triggers an AWS CodePipeline run that runs the fidelity tests before the change is published to the public GitHub repository.

How we keep it secure Because the code is written by agents, an independent security agent reviews changes adversarially, both while the fix is being made and again in the release pipeline as a final check before anything ships.

Security of your own use remains a shared responsibility. We build the emulator to run safely on your machine: it listens only on your own computer by default and rejects requests that aren’t signed with its own keys. You decide where it runs, what data you put in it, and how you test before production. Don’t use the emulator to test whether your application is secure. It doesn’t evaluate AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) policies and resource-based policies the way AWS does, so a request that AWS denies might succeed in the emulator. Keep real credentials out of the environment of your test jobs, and test your security settings and your whole application on AWS before you go to production.

Now available AWS Emulator is generally available today. It has no additional service fee. You pay only for AWS resources when you deploy on AWS. You can install it from RPM or Debian packages on Linux, run it in Docker on macOS and Windows, or build from source, and it works with the AWS SDKs and the AWS CLI once you set environment variables. At launch, it has some limits. It doesn’t evaluate IAM policies the way AWS does, and each emulator acts as a single account, with no cross-account or cross-Region behavior. How closely it matches AWS varies by service and feature. To see how well the emulator covers the services that you use, check the fidelity scores in the AWS Emulator documentation.

If you want to check regional availability, visit the AWS Capabilities by Region page in AWS Builder Center. If you want to call APIs, search documentation, find regional availability, and check troubleshooting about this new feature, try using the AWS MCP Server and plugins with your preferred AI tool.

To get started, visit the AWS Emulator repository on GitHub and see the AWS Emulator documentation.

Updated on November 12, 2026: Added links to the AWS Emulator repository on GitHub.

He helps startups and enterprises build AI-powered applications and modernize with cloud-native architectures. #9972. Simple Sudoku Solver in Verilog

Welcome back to another round of Simple Sudoku Solvers! If you are unfamiliar with the series, I suggest you start with the first post or by perusing the backlog. Last time, in assembly, we told the CPU exactly what to do, one instruction at a time. Today we go one level lower and build the machine directly in Verilog.

Verilog is a hardware description language. You donât write a program that will at some point run on hardware. Instead, you describe a circuit, and the compiler turns that description into gates and flip-flops. Weâll run it in a simulator, because I donât have a Sudoku chip lying around (future work), but the solver is real hardware in the sense that a synthesis tool accepts it and tells us how many gates it would take. Still counts, even with sim2real TBD.

The solver is about 145 lines, plus 40 lines of ceremony to feed it a puzzle and print the result. You can run it with iverilog -o sudoku sudoku.v && vvp sudoku, using Icarus Verilog. I didnât test it anywhere else. As always, the code is on GitHub.

Season three is about solvers, specifications, and constraints, and somehow also about hardware and the lowest of low levels. Thatâs because hardware is possibly the purest version of a specification (and, to be quite honest, because I felt like it).

I think this was the strangest episode so far, for me. I donât mean that in a bad way.

If youâve never read Verilog before, here is what you need for this post.

A module is a circuit with inputs and outputs. wire [8:0] x is a bundle of nine wires, numbered 8 down to 0. reg is a bit of a misnomer: itâs a value we assign in a procedural block, and whether it becomes an actual register is actually dependent on our usage of it.

There are two kinds of blocks we care about. always @* describes combinational logic. Its outputs are a pure function of its inputs, and they change whenever the inputs do. Think of it as a very big expression.

always @(posedge clk), on the other hand, describes sequential logic. It runs once at every rising clock edge, and the <= assignments inside it all happen together at the end of that edge. Thatâs where all our state lives.

for loops exist, but in synthesizable code they are unrolled completely. A loop over 81 cells is 81 copies of its body. Keep that in mind, it will matter. Itâs also very cool, so itâs worth keeping in mind anyway.

The board is the same 81 cells as always, but since hardware doesnât really do arrays of bytes, it is one 324-bit vector, with four bits per cell and 0 for an empty cell:

We have three input wires and output regs (remember, not necessarily registers). Thatâs the whole interface of our chip.

We put a puzzle on the puzzle wires, hold start for one cycle, and wait until done goes high (think in currents). Then, if solved is set, board has the answer. Otherwise, the board is unsolvable.

Reading a cell is a slice, which we wrap in a small function.

Slices work like in many other languages, except that the operators +: and -: encode a direction from the start index. Here, we say âstart at 4 * i and take the next 4 bitsâ.

Units are the 27 rows, columns, and boxes we always care about. We describe them with a function that tells us which cell is the k-th member of unit u:

The first 9 are the rows, then come the columns, and the icky expression at the end there is the box arithmetic with our usual set of magic numbers.

Fun fact: this looks like it does division at runtime, but it doesnât. We only ever call it with constants from unrolled loops, so the synthesis tool computes all of it ahead of time (much like an optimizing compiler would). What is left is just the wiring, and the box arithmetic decides which wires connect.

Like in many previous installments, we track digits as bitmasks. And like in our assembly episode, when itâs convenient we use the trick where digit d lives in bit d, and an empty cell lands in bit 0, which we throw away:

In hardware this is a decoder, four wires in, ten wires out, one of them lights up. Dropping bit 0 is just not connecting it. We donât need a branch, and in this case not even an instruction. These sorts of tricks are annoying the higher up the stack we go, but they come naturally to us when weâre thinking in circuits and currents.

We also need the opposite direction, from a single bit back to a digit, and a popcount:

We are back to having to write our own popcount, regretfully, but it doesnât have to be smart. Itâs a chain of adders in the end, unrolled by our magical synthesis tool again.

This is where Verilog differs from everything else weâve done!

The following block is combinational. Every clock cycle, it looks at the whole board and computes, for all 81 cells at the same time, everything the solver could want to know.

Thatâs quite a few symbols, but it almost looks familiar I think.

For each of the 27 units we or together the digits it contains into seen. While we do that, we check if a digit was already there, and if so, the unit has a clash. No other solver in the series has needed this check so far, and youâll see in a minute why we need it now. Hint: it has to do with the parallel nature of the system.

The candidates are the usual not-yet-taken numbers, and we compute them for all cells. We end up with four answers:

This reads much like the solver loop weâve written many times, but it works completely differently, because there is no loop. The circuit that is synthesized has 81 candidate calculators and a long chain of comparators for the minimum that are all settling at once.

Why the clash check? Here, because of parallelism, forced fills in every forced cell in the same cycle. If two cells in the same unit are both set to the same number, we write both of those in the same cycle and nothing checks at the end. Instead, we check the unit for duplicates at the next cycle, and treat a clash like any other unsolvable branch.

So weâve successfully parallelized our work, including our mistakes! Fun!

Since there is no recursion, the search becomes a state machine with three states:

RUN propagates and branches, BACK backtracks, and HALT is the stop condition.

For backtracking we need a stack. The entry has the board before a guess, the cell we guessed in, and the candidates we havenât tried yet:

Every guess fills at least one cell, so the search canât go deeper than 81, and 81 entries are enough to hold our search tree. Math! Logic!

Unfortunately, we have to pay for every entry in hardware, no matter if we end up using it or not.

I originally called the second array cell, but it turns out cell is a reserved word in Verilog. Itâs used for configurations, which I had never heard of before. Shows what I know. Iâm just documenting this because where is a bit of an odd name, I think, but I didnât think to pull out the thesaurus1.

Anyway, time to look at the actual states.

Side note: the first cycle is spent initializing, then we fall through to our case structure.

RUN is our whole solver as an if chain. If the board is dead, we backtrack. If there are forced cells, we fill all of them and come back next cycle to continue our work. If the board is full, weâre done and set HALT and all our stopping variables.

Otherwise we dance. pick is the candidate mask of the MRV cell:

We push the current board, the cell, and the remaining candidates, and then write the lowest candidate into the board. pick & -pick isolates the lowest set bit, and pick & (pick - 1) clears it, so together they split the mask into what to try now vs.Â what to try later. Thatâs my official favorite trick from the last episode making a second appearance as a subtractor and a row of and gates.

This is also the place that tripped me up most when I was learning Verilog for this: all of these <= assignments happen together at the clock edge. We write board into the stack and change one cell of board in the same cycle, and the stack still gets the old board, because everything on the right-hand side was read before the edge. The timing is very explicit, and my intuitions are still very much developing.

The BACK state looks at the top of the stack:

If the stack is empty, weâve tried everything, and there is no solution.

If the top entry has no candidates left, we pop it and stay in BACK, so the next cycle looks at the entry below. So we do one backtracking step per cycle, at worst 81 times. This seems wasteful at first, but itâs actually beautiful in its simplicity I find.

Otherwise we restore the saved board, try the next candidate, and go back to RUN. The entry stays on the stack with one fewer candidate, ready to come back if this oneâs a dud, too.

This, too, is the same copy-and-restore dance number from assembly, but itâs copying a board in one cycle. A register that is 324 bits wide is just 324 flip-flops that all load at the same time. If you design the board you can do whatever, it turns out.

And thatâs it! Weâve solved the board!

Our usual hard puzzle takes 7,639 cycles. The puzzles from the repository take between 5 cycles (easy) and 411 cycles (evil), and a puzzle with two 8s in the first row is rejected in 2 cycles, because the clash check catches it right away.

That number is hard to compare with the other episodes. If the circuit ran at 1 MHz, 7,639 cycles would be about 7.5 milliseconds. But I havenât placed and routed it, so I donât know how fast it could really be made2. The 81 comparator chain we built above would probably be the limit, but again, I have no intuitions on how to measure this.

The simulation, on the other hand, is slow. Icarus simulates every wire of that circuit on every cycle, and running the hard puzzle takes about 11 seconds on my machine. That makes it the slowest solver in the series by a wide margin, beating even Agda. Thatâs not a fair comparison, but I think itâs funny anyway, because we came to the land of speed and wires and ended up with the slowest simulations of the series.

As for size, I let the genie guide me and ran the solver through Yosys targeting Lattice iCE40, a family of small FPGAs that hobbyists like. It comes out at about 35,000 lookup tables and 28,000 flip-flops, almost all in the stack. That is a lot more than any iCE40 chip Iâve found has, so weâd need a bigger FPGA, or a stack in block RAM, which would cost us a cycle per access.

If you want to build this circuit, be my guest! Do send pictures and/or measurements, though, please.

We built a Sudoku solver out of (simulated) wires and flip-flops, and made the thing nicely parallel. Through our little state machine, we also added a new tool to our bag of tricks. Time will tell if we need it again.

I still think this one fits the season better than it might have seemed on paper. We really did specify Sudoku in hardware, in a way, in a very lop-sided chip.

In the next episode, we stop writing search code entirely once again: we hand the constraints to z3 and let it find the answer for us, much like in Prolog and miniKanren, but differently. See you there!

2. Synthesis turns the description into gates. Placing and routing then decide where on the chip each gate goes and how the wires run between them, and only then do you know how long a signal takes to get through the slowest path, which sets the maximum clock speed through the annoyances of physics. I didnât do that step by hand, and I donât know whether there is a tool for doing it automatically for me.

#9970. AWS Weekly Roundup: AWS Nitro Sandboxes, AWS Emulator, and more (November 16, 2026)

AWS is the world's most comprehensive cloud, enabling organizations to accelerate innovation, reduce costs, and scale more efficiently

Migrate to modernize → Modernize to unlock data → unlock data to run AI

Get started with one of these featured services or browse all

From startups to enterprises, find AWS solutions scaled to your needs. Access tailored resources, pricing models, and support levels.

A second delivery of the same message can reveal more about an application than its happy-path demo. I like tools that make those cases easier to investigate while a change is still small. Last week’s launch of AWS Emulator brings part of that work onto your own machine: developers and coding agents can exercise AWS API interactions, inspect results, and try again without provisioning cloud resources for every attempt.

I wrote about the Emulator’s launch last week, and it’s my main highlight in this edition. There are also new ways to isolate workloads on shared infrastructure, give an agent narrowly scoped access to a backend, and prepare search applications for a regional disruption. Now, let’s get into this week’s AWS news…

AWS Emulator runs locally alongside your code and development tools. Image: AWS.

HeadlinesTest your applications against AWS locally with AWS Emulator introduces a generally available local environment for AWS API interactions. Point the AWS CLI or AWS SDKs at its HTTPS endpoint, and your application keeps its normal SDK calls. The walkthrough shows a coding agent creating an Amazon DynamoDB table, writing an item, and reading it back. You don’t need an AWS account for emulated operations, and there is no additional service fee. The getting-started guide covers Linux packages, Docker for macOS and Windows, and agent-assisted setup; the source is on GitHub.

What I like is giving an agent concrete feedback while it works: run calls, inspect results, and revise the code. Matt Wood’s perspective on feedback for coding agents explores why that loop matters. Check the published fidelity results for your operations, because coverage varies and unimplemented calls return HTTP 501. The emulator doesn’t reproduce IAM and resource-policy enforcement or cross-account and cross-Region behavior, so test the complete application and its security configuration on AWS before production.

AWS Nitro Sandboxes bring hardware isolation to pods, tasks, and VMs. You can give an Amazon EKS pod or Amazon ECS task its own VM boundary while sharing an Amazon EC2 instance. That is useful for tenant workloads, build jobs, and agents executing generated code. Isolated mode separates workloads from their neighbors; confidential mode adds protection from node operators and cryptographic attestation. The Compute Blog deep dive explains both modes and their integrations. Nitro Sandboxes have no additional charge on supported instances; EC2 and applicable EKS Auto Mode or ECS Managed Instances fees still apply.

Last week’s launches Here are some launches and updates from this past week that caught my attention:

Amazon Cognito supports OAuth 2.0 token exchange – You can now exchange a user’s token for one scoped to a downstream service in Amazon Cognito. The derived token can have narrower permissions and a single audience, with no refresh token; supplying an actor token also identifies the intermediary in an act claim. For an agent calling a backend on someone’s behalf, that makes delegation more explicit without forwarding the original token. The feature is available on Essentials and Plus plans in all Cognito Regions.

Claude Fable 5.2 is available on AWS – You can access the model through Amazon Bedrock or Claude Platform on AWS. Anthropic positions it as its most capable generally available model for technical work, including extended engineering tasks, scientific research, and quantitative finance. Bedrock has model-specific retention requirements: Fable 5.2 traffic is retained for up to 30 days for abuse detection, with a temporary zero-retention exception for eligible internal use.

Amazon ElastiCache Serverless adds search and aggregations – You can now combine vector, full-text, and hybrid search with server-side aggregations in Amazon ElastiCache Serverless for Valkey. That gives product discovery, recommendations, and agent-memory retrieval another option for querying frequently changing data. The capability requires Valkey 9, so create a compatible cache or upgrade an existing one. It is available in commercial Regions, AWS GovCloud (US), and the AWS European Sovereign Cloud.

Amazon OpenSearch Service adds managed cross-Region disaster recovery – You can now pair Amazon OpenSearch Service domains running version 3.7 or later in two Regions within one account. AWS specifies recovery objectives under one minute for data loss and under 20 minutes for recovery time. Planned switchovers preserve all writes; unplanned failovers can lose unreplicated data. The deep dive covers the remaining work: keeping configuration aligned and redirecting application writes after switching roles, plus secondary-domain and data-transfer charges.

Amazon CloudWatch Logs adds account-level retention policies – You can now set retention across all log groups or groups matching a name prefix in Amazon CloudWatch, with policies covering existing groups or only new ones. When policies overlap, the longest retention period applies. A platform team can set a baseline and retain security logs longer without updating every group individually. The feature has no additional charge and is available in commercial Regions except Middle East (Bahrain) and Middle East (UAE).

The next generation AgentCore runtime is now the default – New Amazon Bedrock AgentCore runtimes now use the next-generation runtime by default, so agent sessions start in under 2 seconds, scale up to 8 vCPU and 32 GB, scale to zero when idle, and bill up to 68% less memory, while each session still runs in its own isolated microVM.

For a full list of AWS announcements, be sure to keep an eye on the What’s New with AWS page.

Other AWS news Here are some additional posts and resources that you might find interesting:

Optimizing cost per task and proving agent ROI on Amazon Bedrock – This guide follows an agent’s cost through repeated calls, reasoning, caching, and human review. I like its emphasis on measuring a completed task and comparing outcomes against a documented baseline. Its worked prices are illustrative; use your own workload and reconcile estimated costs with billing data.

How Zillow runs 100 million daily notifications on AWS Step Functions – Zillow describes reusable content modules and configuration-driven AWS Step Functions Express Workflows for more than 100 million daily notifications. The useful engineering details include idempotent modules, batching, campaign isolation, and testing expressions with the TestState API before deployment. Those patterns apply well beyond notification systems.

Upcoming AWS events Check your calendar and sign up for upcoming AWS events:

AWS re:Invent – Join the community in Las Vegas from November 30 to December 4. Browse more than 2,200 sessions, including workshops and deep dives, or register for the free livestream to follow keynotes and selected sessions remotely.

AWS Community Days – Find community-led technical talks, workshops, and hands-on learning near you. Check each organizer’s page for current dates and registration details.

Join the AWS Builder Center to connect with builders, share solutions, and access content that supports your development. Browse here for upcoming AWS-led in-person and virtual events and developer-focused events.

That’s all for this week. Check back next Monday for another Weekly Roundup!

This post is part of our Weekly Roundup series. Check back each week for a quick roundup of interesting news and announcements from AWS!

#9963. AWS Lambda now supports GPU instances for Event Functions on Lambda Managed Instances

AWS is the world's most comprehensive cloud, enabling organizations to accelerate innovation, reduce costs, and scale more efficiently

Migrate to modernize → Modernize to unlock data → unlock data to run AI

Get started with one of these featured services or browse all

From startups to enterprises, find AWS solutions scaled to your needs. Access tailored resources, pricing models, and support levels.

GPU support is now available for EC2 G-series GPU instances for Event Functions running on AWS Lambda Managed Instances (LMI). You can now run GPU-accelerated workloads, including machine learning inference, media processing, rendering, and scientific computing, on GPU instances with serverless simplicity. GPU-accelerated functions are deployed as container (Open Container Initiative, OCI) images. You build an OCI image, point the function at it, and let Lambda handle provisioning, scaling, and event integration. There are no GPU drivers, CUDA versions, or AMIs to reconcile, and no clusters or device plugins to operate. GPU-accelerated functions run on the same Lambda Managed Instances foundation that already gives you Amazon EC2 pricing and specialized compute without managing servers.

Why customers need this Customers keep asking to run GPU workloads with the simplicity of serverless. Building on self-managed GPU infrastructure means selecting instances, installing and reconciling GPU drivers and CUDA libraries, planning capacity, writing scaling logic, and hand-building the event integrations that connect the GPU step to the rest of the application. Serverless GPU services that hide that work often sit outside your AWS environment, with no native event sources, identity, or networking.

Cost is the second problem. GPUs are expensive, and utilization is usually low because a single workload rarely saturates a GPU. A small inference task can leave most of a provisioned GPU idle while you pay for the whole thing.

This feature closes both gaps. You bring a function, and Lambda runs it on a GPU in minutes, triggered by the same AWS events as any other Lambda Event Function, billed and secured the same way. It also maximizes utilization of every GPU you pay for, by consolidating functions onto instances and keeping GPUs busy across concurrent requests.

What you can build You can run both AI/ML inference and non-ML workloads using GPU-accelerated compute on Lambda Managed Instances. This capability is optimized for inference rather than training, and custom models rather than large foundation models already available on services like Amazon Bedrock. Common workloads include:

Part of the Lambda programming model A GPU-accelerated function is one step in a larger application, and it composes with the rest of Lambda. Lambda durable functions orchestrate multi-step, long-running workflows around the GPU step, with checkpointing and automatic recovery. Lambda MicroVMs run untrusted or model-generated code in isolated, stateful sandboxes. In an agentic workload, a MicroVM executes the tool-use logic on CPU, then calls a GPU-accelerated function running on Lambda Managed Instances for inference.

GPU-accelerated functions also support the extended function timeout on Lambda Managed Instances, up to 90 minutes for asynchronous and event source mapping invocations, so you can run batch and other long-running GPU jobs, such as media transcoding or multi-step inference, without re-architecting. GPU-accelerated functions support container images up to 32 GB (10 GB per file), up to 32 GB of ephemeral storage, 2,048 to 32,768 MB of memory, 3 to 48 GB of accelerator memory, up to 48 concurrent requests per execution environment, and up to 15,000 vCPUs per capacity provider.

Let’s try it out To show what this looks like in practice, I deployed an open-source large language model (LLM) from Hugging Face as a Lambda function and sent it a prompt. With the vLLM base image from Lambda, I only set the Hugging Face model ID in the MODEL_ID environment variable, without writing any inference code. I used Qwen/Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct, a small instruction-tuned model that suits in-application tasks such as summarization, classification, and extraction. The flow has four steps: create a capacity provider, build and push the container image, create a function from that image, then publish and invoke. Before you begin, request an increase to your G-series instance quota (listed as Running On-Demand G and VT instances), because new accounts might start with a quota of 0. For more information, see On-Demand Instance quotas.

First, I created a capacity provider, where I specify the GPU instance types Lambda can use and let it auto-scale. Listing several instance types lets Lambda pick the most cost-effective one that is available and fall back across generations when capacity is tight.

The Lambda console shows the new capacity provider, lmi-gpu-cp, in the Active state. Note the VPC configuration with its subnets and security group.

Figure 1: The capacity provider is Active, with its VPC configuration.

Next, I built the container image. Lambda provides a curated vLLM base image that includes the vLLM inference server, PyTorch, Transformers, and the CUDA toolkit, along with a runtime interface client that supports concurrent invocations. The image serves the model for me, so I don’t write a handler or any inference server code. My entire Dockerfile is one line:

After pushing the image to Amazon ECR, I created the function. I chose the model with the MODEL_ID environment variable, which accepts a Hugging Face or ModelScope repository, an Amazon S3 location, or a local path. Lambda downloads the model, manages GPU memory, and serves requests. Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct is a public model, so I didn’t need a Hugging Face token. For private or gated models, or to get higher download rate limits, you can also set HF_TOKEN.

GPU-accelerated functions use AcceleratorConfig to request accelerator memory. AcceleratorMemorySize is the minimum GPU memory the function needs, and Lambda places the execution environment on the smallest available GPU that meets it, so the GPU you get can have more memory than you requested. I set PerExecutionEnvironmentMaxConcurrency to 4, the default. The vLLM server batches concurrent requests on the GPU, so invocations share one copy of the model and the GPU stays busy. I also set ExecutionEnvironmentMemoryGiBPerVCpu to 4, which gives the function the 16,384 MB of memory and 4 vCPUs it needs while leaving capacity on the 2xlarge instance for Lambda’s management components.

The function overview shows what makes this a GPU-accelerated function: the attached capacity provider that supplies the GPU instances and the vLLM container image deployed from Amazon ECR, all wired into the same function model you already use.

Figure 2: The lmi-gpu-inference function overview, showing the attached capacity provider and the vLLM container image deployed from Amazon ECR.

Functions on Lambda Managed Instances run from a published version, so I published one. Publishing provisions the execution environments, and each one downloads the model weights and warms up the engine before the version becomes active. The cold start happens during the publish step, so the first caller doesn’t wait for it.

Then I sent the model a prompt. The payload is a standard OpenAI request body: a messages array routes to chat completions, and a prompt field routes to text completions.

The model answered from a GPU inside the Lambda execution environment, and the response is a standard OpenAI completion object, so any OpenAI-compatible client works with it.

Four concurrent invocations finished in about the same time as a single one, on one execution environment that shares one copy of the model in GPU memory. From a Hugging Face model ID to a live, OpenAI-compatible GPU endpoint took about 10 minutes, most of it unattended while Lambda provisioned capacity and warmed up the model.

That’s a working LLM endpoint with no inference server code, no GPU drivers, and no cluster to manage. To try a different model, I update MODEL_ID and publish a new version, with no image rebuild. Each version is an immutable snapshot, so different models can run side by side as separate versions. It is also a Lambda Event Function, so I can trigger it from an Amazon SQS queue to process documents in batches, put Amazon API Gateway in front of it, or call it as the inference step in a Lambda durable functions workflow.

For production, copy the model weights to an S3 bucket in the same Region, point MODEL_ID at that bucket, and set VLLM_LOAD_FORMAT=runai_streamer so the weights stream straight into memory. This gives faster starts and removes the dependency on the Hugging Face Hub. For more guidance, see the best practices for running inference workloads. Beyond LLM inference, you can also run custom ML inference, media processing, and other GPU workloads. See the Lambda documentation for best practices.

The configuration tab shows the settings that matter for a GPU-accelerated function: 16,384 MB of memory, the 15-minute timeout, and 32 GB of ephemeral storage for the downloaded weights, alongside the function-level capacity provider settings: per-environment concurrency of 4, the 4:1 memory-to-vCPU ratio, and 16 GB of accelerator memory.

Figure 3: The function’s configuration, including memory, timeout, and 32 GB of ephemeral storage, and the function-level capacity provider settings: per-environment concurrency, the memory-to-vCPU ratio, and accelerator memory.

When you finish testing, delete the function and then the capacity provider so that Lambda stops the GPU instances and you stop paying for them.

How it works The capabilities below are what you get out of the box, each one removing GPU work you would otherwise own.

Skip the GPU software setup. Curated base images ship with the frameworks and tools handled for you, so you do not install or reconcile them: base:cuda (CUDA toolkit and runtime), cupy:cuda (CuPy, NumPy, SciPy, Pandas, Numba), pytorch:cuda (PyTorch, torchvision, torchaudio, transformers, FFmpeg), and serving images vllm:cuda and sglang:cuda. Use them directly, extend them, or bring a fully custom image.

No GPU infrastructure to operate. Lambda handles driver compatibility, provisioning, routing, and load balancing, so you ship functions instead of running GPU fleets. Deploy with the same Console, CLI, AWS CloudFormation, AWS CDK, AWS SAM, and Terraform workflow as any Lambda Event Function.

Trigger GPU work from any AWS event. The same 200+ event sources that trigger Event Functions, including Amazon S3, Amazon SQS, Amazon API Gateway, and Amazon EventBridge, trigger GPU-accelerated functions directly, with the same scaling, error handling, and retries. No custom integration code.

Serve concurrent requests on each GPU. Each execution environment can process multiple concurrent invocations on the same GPU, which you control with the per-environment concurrency setting. Raising it packs more requests onto each GPU instance to drive utilization up, so you get more throughput from the capacity you already pay for.

Multiple instance types. Specify multiple instance types or generations, and Lambda selects the most cost-effective available option and falls back across your list to reduce Insufficient Capacity Errors.

Capacity options. GPU instances run as Amazon EC2 On-Demand instances, and your existing Savings Plans and Reserved Instances apply. For predictable GPU availability, create an EC2 On-Demand Capacity Reservation (ODCR) that matches your capacity provider configuration, and Lambda uses that reserved capacity automatically.

Large container images and storage. Container images up to 32 GB are supported, along with up to 32 GB of NVMe ephemeral storage in /tmp. Seekable OCI (SOCI) lazy loading lets your function begin executing before the full image is downloaded, which reduces execution environment startup time by up to 70%.

See GPU usage without extra setup. GPU utilization, GPU memory utilization, GPU memory used, and GPU power utilization appear alongside standard function metrics in Amazon CloudWatch and in the AWS Lambda console.

After invoking the function, the console surfaces the GPU-specific metrics next to the standard ones. Track GPU utilization, GPU memory utilization, GPU memory used, and GPU power utilization to see how much of the accelerator each invocation actually uses, which is the signal that drives both auto-scaling and cost.

Figure 4: GPU utilization, GPU memory utilization, GPU memory used, and GPU power utilization for the vLLM function under concurrent load.

Pricing and availability This feature is generally available today, supporting the Amazon EC2 G-series (G4dn, G5, G6, G6f, Gr6, Gr6f, G6e) at launch, with more instance families to come. You pay the underlying EC2 instance fee (eligible for Savings Plans and Reserved Instances), plus a 9.75 percent management fee for GPU instances, and the standard Lambda request fee of $0.20 per million requests. For pricing and Region availability, see AWS Lambda pricing.

You can also build with your AI coding assistants and agents: explore the Builder Center and connect your tools with the Agent Toolkit for AWS, which bundles the AWS MCP Server and curated agent skills.

To get started, visit the AWS Lambda console and see the GPU-accelerated functions documentation.

He helps startups and enterprises build AI-powered applications and modernize with cloud-native architectures. #9961. The Strength of the Record

The computer is a curious gadget. It is one of few human inventions which can exist purely — yet accurately — in the imagination. Prior to the existence of a real computing machine, mathematicians could hypothesize how it might behave. They even understood the unbounded, fractal potential of computers: If human beings have machines for computation we also have the atom of computation and we can recombine these atoms to great effect. Our largest and most complex computers were borne of tiny, simple computing components.

Cixin Liu visualized this agglomeration beautifully in The Three-Body Problem. Liu imagines the characters of his book playing an open-world, emergent MMORPG. The players, who know nothing about computer design, create a functional computer in-game (a la Minecraft) through the composition of thirty million other players, with each of those thirty million individuals acting as a computational gate. An expanse of desert acts as Liu’s silicon wafer under the gates of his meat computer. Quite naturally, the username of the player who creates the computer is Von Neumann.

Whatever hardware brings a computer to life — whether soldiers in the desert or transistors on silicon — its various parts require names. Liu’s fantasy human computer has registers, stack memory, a system bus, and a hard drive. Most of his components consist of people raising and lowering flags to control the flow of data, with one exception. Scholars with notepads comprise the hard disk — a notion we’ll revisit in a moment.

Liu’s component names all seem obvious to us, due to their twenty-first century ubiquity. But why these names? If I had never heard of a computer before, would I consider stack memory emblematic of a stack of cards or would the name seem arbitrary? When we pick apart a label like "system bus", and thus the etymology of "omnibus", we begin to see the exercise of naming things in two parts. The first, and more obvious, is the coining of terms. The more important second part is the construction of metaphors.

We only need to revisit some Today Show clips from 1994 to recall how alien computers and computer networks were just three decades ago. In 1991 a computer was a magical box of infinite possibility. A computer — a real computing machine — is by its very nature an abstract thing and thus has always been so much more than a better calculator or a fancier accounting ledger. And yet, paradoxically, that’s precisely how we use computers today. Computers coordinate the most mundane aspects of the global economy, send me a message when my library book is due, or record a family’s new home in the government’s Land Titles database. The sprawling mycelium of computing devices across the globe behave, in aggregate, much more like the robots of retrofuturism than any of us are likely to acknowledge. The robots take us shopping and help us with video calls to our aging parents. The robots are ubiquitous, invisible, and heart-breakingly banal.

Our prosaic robots exist at every layer. The robot is the L2 cache, Linux, and Google Maps. Is it little wonder that we, the techno-elite, construct some brittle metaphors as we climb from XOR gates and system buses to the abstractions that reach the fingertips of the humans? Along the way, we hold on to some outdated metaphors from earlier days of computing. EOT (End-of-Tape) markers show up less commonly in software these days but a modern programmer won’t blink an eye at an EOF (End-of-File) marker of the same lineage. As computers entered the mainstream, "directories" of files were given the thin coat of paint known as "folders", producing the increasingly-peculiar physical metaphor of putting your files inside of folders inside of folders inside of folders. The "filing cabinet" metaphor had a more timely death. My last memory of the filing cabinet is Windows for Workgroups.

Of course, we need not restrict ourselves to the tangible world of buttons, files, and folders. We programmers kick ourselves with broken metaphors all the time while programming the robot’s innards. Remember when we used "object-relational mapping" libraries to write objects to disk? Those were heady days, weren’t they? [1] I still remember my first glimpse of the Rails ActiveRecord implementation. has_many :simply_darling_little_macros was an epiphany back in 2004 for those of us stuck wiring the fields in our POJOs to database columns by hand like mid-century telephone operators hard-wiring networks of voices, one at a time. Yessir. ORM was a thing of beauty, compared to her contemporaries. Every day at 8:00 AM I would grab a steaming cup of loam-flavoured American drip coffee and sit back to enjoy the DHH Show — marveling at his juxtapositions: a quagmire of Spring XML against his elegant Ruby macros. But that’s not what I’m talking about.

The real question is: Why were we mapping anything at all? Why was anything required to save an object / record / document to disk beyond this?

Today, ActiveRecord is void. Mapping objects into databases is outmoded. The idea has a certain appeal, no doubt. I record (verb) my records (noun) to disk. When they are read back into memory via has_one :superfluous_abstraction the virtual machine makes them active — singing, dancing, and procreating through the object lifecycle — until they are recorded back into Postgres. But this act of recording doesn’t necessitate mapping. Object mapping is a broken metaphor.

In fact, object mapping is a broken metaphor built on broken metaphors. We have a User object in memory we want to save to disk. That’s all. Instead of a command equivalent to "computer, save the user" we are met with forty years' worth of anachronisms. We must worry about join tables, floating point value coercion, and whether or not our TIMESTAMP columns are automatic.

The mapping is a symptom; the anachronism is the disease. Our objects can and should maintain symmetry with the database unless we tell them otherwise. To do so, we must choose a new storage metaphor for the next forty years.

End users understand the metaphors of buttons, folders, and desktops as user interfaces. So it is for us developers and our database metaphors. There is some surface area to a database that allows us to store, query, and listen. This is our user interface. It is also our storage metaphor.

Storage metaphors come in three broad structural categories: rows in tables, documents in trees, triples in graphs. These structures, in turn, are bound to a three-dimensional field. Our X-axis is schema, from hard to soft, our Y-axis is depth, from flat to nested, and our Z-axis is shape repetition, from regular to unique. Positioned within this cube, any given structure represents the form of our database.

I was fifteen years old in 1996. My highschool had an "Information Processing" class for Grade 10 students, from which I distinctly remember an argument between a close friend and the teacher while they stooped over a PowerMac running ClarisWorks. My friend insisted that learning a spreadsheet was unnecessary since the word processor already provided "tables". Although my teacher understood that the word processor’s tables were insufficient for accounting, I do remember his argument eventually came down to "just trust me on this one" rather than diving into the semantics of ClarisWorks' internal data representation. My friend’s confusion was only exacerbated the following week when a desktop database was added to the mix. In his mind, a table is a table is a table.

It’s easy to see where this confusion comes from. Most people do not care what a computer thinks about rows in a table. A table is an intuitive concept, even to children. But we all know, just as my teacher understood, that text in an arbitrary table is effectively meaningless, text in a spreadsheet table is meaningful but unconstrained, and text in a database is constrained by datatype. When your tables have constraints you can build schema, views, atomic writes, and table-to-table relationships on top of them. That’s powerful stuff.

Looking back at Cixin Liu’s "hard drive" comprised of scholars with notepads, our confidence in the meat computer is likely to go up if we can put some hard limitations on what kinds of data the scholars are allowed to write, and where. The scholar who writes whatever she wants wherever she wants is not a very useful component. She must adhere to the sensibilities of the computer.

Tables are powerful precisely because of their handicaps. They are not mathematically perfect constructions sent to us from the Heavens or Harvard. [3] Instead, they are intuitive, flat, and readily map to business processes. Tables have served us well for three or four decades and most businesses can still survive on software built with tables alone. For a while. Businesses in the 1990s could survive on paper for a while, too.

Skip ahead nearly a decade to 2004. I stumbled across Prevayler during my years at University. "10,000 times faster than Oracle? This thing is going to be huge," I thought. We all know how that turned out. Years later when my younger colleagues were getting excited about Couch and MongoDB, I found myself put off by the lack of standard querying and the entire shoot-from-the-hip attitude document databases were pitching. "Schemaless! No SQL! Just shove things in the database and figure it out later!" No thanks.

Over a decade later, I don’t know of a single object database or document database in those ex-colleagues' production systems. Everyone uses Postgres. Why?

Object DBs simply never took off. An object isn’t a simple or intuitive concept; an object is type-matching dynamic dispatch implemented over a collection of closures which in turn share a second collection of lexically-bound variables which themselves are — you guessed it — more objects. [4] These trees of objects are nested indefinitely. Many of us have made a career out of object-oriented programming but the essence of an object is message passing, not structs for disk serialization.

Document DBs, on the other hand, were not such a bad idea. They were just poorly implemented. Standard query languages? Nope. Schemaless? Nope. Relationships? Not really. Append-only, immutable data? That gets pretty expensive when you denormalize all your records into a deeply-nested rat’s nest.

Developers want languages built on research and standards. Even a fragmented standard like SQL is better than a homebrew query language. MongoDB lacked basic joins until version 3.2 but this was an honest mistake. MongoDB engineers believed their customers could survive on schemaless, denormalized data with no relationships. We now know this isn’t true. All databases have schema. [5] All databases have relationships. [6] Our schema and relationships may be implicit but they are truths we must face.

Neo4j, on the other hand, is a document database that actually works. Neo4j is a property graph and property graphs do not pretend relational data doesn’t exist — or that it exists but somehow isn’t important. Unfortunately, Neo4j has its own homebrew query language, Cypher, with its own baggage. Although an open standard since 2017, Cypher queries are difficult to compose because the language lacks a foundation in logic:

Rather than hide behind a deeply-nested document model or inglorious query languages, we can put our faith in decades of research. Computer Science tends to invent things long before they hit the market so it’s likely a high-caliber document store need not invent anything from scratch. An immutable document store supported by a well-understood query language for traversing relationships would feel natural to users and developers alike — the best parts of MongoDB and Neo4j without the dross.

Skip ahead another decade to 2014. Clojure already won my heart prior to its 1.0 release in 2009. By 2014 I was building a company on it. I was excited about the possibility of Clojure-style simplicity in database form: The triple-store.

Roughly, there are two categories of triples: RDF triples, which attempt to encode relationship semantics, and EAV triples, which only encode the relationship. A semantic triple might look something like [Bob belongs_to CommunistParty] where an EAV triple is more likely to take the shape [Bob :party CommunistParty]. Rather than debate the semantics of semantic triples, we’ll treat them as loosely equivalent for this story. Caveat lector.

My team was immediately attracted to triples. The declarative logic of Datalog, with its Prolog origins, felt like the perfect way to ask questions of a database. Having never worked with triple-stores before, there was a purity to EAV triples none of us had ever imagined possible during our career with relational databases. An immutable store of pure facts? Count us in!

Alas. Just as a child grows up and learns her parents and teachers are not infallible, so does the star-struck developer seduced by the siren song of purity. I know better now. These days, when I read my friend Abhinav’s Haskell articles, full of beautiful and orderly code, I look back on my time with the triples and remind myself that purity can be a dangerous waste of time. Rather than squandering my finite time on this planet searching for the bottom of the purity rabbit hole, I instead watch Haskell from afar with profound respect and terror.

Back in 2014 our triple-store of choice had a hard schema, not unlike the schema definitions in most relational databases. However, it went so much deeper than that. Creating schema for our facts felt like Carl Sagan’s famous quote, reified: "If you wish to make an apple pie from scratch, you must first invent the universe." We really wanted to build our system out of triples but it felt as though we were bootstrapping the universe just to get to square one. Square one, as it turns out, is simply:

We found that bootstrapping wasn’t our only challenge. Schema or no schema, triples are not really natural. Beautiful, yes. Pure, yes. Natural, no. Try as we might, the team never had the epiphany with triples we had each experienced with Clojure.

In retrospect, it feels as though there must be an underlying reason RDF has never enjoyed general database success. Despite more than two decades of research and implementation, RDF remains the storage metaphor of museum artefacts and government statistics. [7] [8] The elevation of purity above all else is a certainly one problem with triples. Their true deficiency, however, is hidden in plain sight: triples by their very nature only describe relationships. Despite their name, relational databases consign the very notion of a "relationship" to the realm of the derivative. Triples have the opposite problem. Triples treat nouns as second-class citizens.

What exactly is a "record"? To understand the record completely, we must look back over the history of computers, back over businesses which predate computers, and back over all of recorded human history. Before we take that trip, though, let’s quickly read the first dictionary entry:

a thing constituting a piece of evidence about the past, especially an account kept in writing or some other permanent form

Computer Scientists will understand: "evidence about the past" is equivalent to "facts on a timeline" and "permanent form" is a synonym for "immutable data".

Once upon a time in computing history, tapes were composed of files which were composed of records. It could be argued that the "record" is actually the most natural of the three, given that humans have been organizing information into records since long before the computer. Sometimes those records were flat rows in an accountant’s ledger but they were often written on card stock:

These sorts of records can be seen for hundreds of years into humanity’s past, at least as far back as the double-entry bookkeeping of 14th Century Venice. It could even be argued that all three storage metaphors we’ve examined so far — the table, the document, and the triple — can claim the title of "record".

But relational databases fail the dictionary definition. Most lack a meaningful, first-class representation of time with which to view the past. The flip side of that coin is the absence of immutability. If you want immutable records for your inventory table you are often stuck managing an inventory_audits table in the application tier…​ wastefully duplicating the built-in Write-Ahead Log of your database in the process.

Triples fail our mental model instead. The client record card is natural. Specifying each individual fact about your client is not. If we want to see that natural record, triples force synecdoche on us. We must ascribe meaning to identities so triples like [Bob has_email "bob@newhart.com"] and [Bob has_phone +15551234567] can be glued together into "Bob". The truth is, there is no "Bob" — only facts about Bob. If triples are to say anything about the form of the data they contain, we must slather them in complicated ontologies.

It is possible to find a middle path between hard, flat rows in tables and infinitely malleable triples. Surprisingly, documents are that middle path.

"Flat is better than nested" is a guideline, not a rule. If we can employ nesting conservatively, the storage metaphor of "documents" can avoid the MongoDB rat’s nest. If we add a standard query language to that, we may really be on to something.

The Client Record Card from a few paragraphs ago is a useful visual aid — it is both a record and a document. "Address" is embedded within the card but the physical constraints of the card prevent us from nesting nests of nests the same way we enjoy foldering folders of folders. Nothing crazy is happening.

Any developer who has sent or received data over an HTTP API in the past ten years is already accustomed to this sort of document. We can all imagine encoding this card in JSON. Nothing crazy will happen.

To ensure nothing crazy will ever happen, our storage metaphor of "documents" must play by the rules. The dictionary says our database must store immutable facts on a timeline. [9] Computer Science says our database must speak a standard query language. Our experience and intuition says our database should provide us lightweight references between our documents and discourage deep nesting.

These are not abstruse or mystical ideas, but they do demand a reappraisal of the database. We can’t just tack immutability onto MongoDB or temporality onto Postgres. [10] We must rebuild the foundation. We must record a graph of immutable facts on a timeline tolerant of growth and query them by time-aware logic. That’s a mouthful, so let’s just call it a Record. This is the new metaphor.

Liu’s scholars in the desert would do precisely this. Each scholar’s document may refer to another scholar’s document. The system (and the user) must be able to read the documents — consistently. Given enough paper, the scholars would never scribble out old documents and rewrite them. Instead, they would maintain a record of every document they’d ever written, ordered by date. The documents are the audit log. Whether we say record or document, the storage metaphor is the user interface for the scholars, just as it is for us.

A copy of this article can always be found at this permanent URL: https://opencrux.com/articles/strength-of-the-record.html
